In brief, the deficit from 1897 to 1909 on the Prince Edward Island railway has averaged $76,100 per year. The capital expenditure has been $4,508,461, an average of $347,000 each year. The capital cost of the road was $3,740,000 in 1897; the interest on it at 4 per cent would be $149,600, the deficit was $236,606. In 1909 the capital cost was $8,259,033, the interest $a31,360, the deficit was $89,001, the burden $420,370, showing the same sinister gain in the burden of that railway under the management of the Minister of Railways.
Now if we ask ourselves why it is that the Intercolonial cannot be made to pay, is there anything in its circumstances that prevents it? Look at the Intercolonial. It passes through a well populated country. It has on its line, commencing with Sydney and Halifax, the towns in Nova Scotia, with St. John and the towns along the north shore, coming up into Quebec, and making its terminus in the city of Montreal, favoured with population, favoured with business which, taken in connection with its tourist capabilities, certainly make it a road which ought to pay at least its working expenses, and the improvement put upon it. No interest paid, no dividend paid, $33,000,000 of capital expenditure and a deficit of $3,481,000-even under these conditions of no interest and no dividend. It is*

simply a plain matter of business management. It can be made to pay, only this government does not seem to be working in that line. Then, what has happened? Not content with running the Intercolonial railway in that way, these gentlemen have come down and they have pledged $26,900,000 of the people's money to build a parallel and competing line of railway from the city of Quebec down to Moncton. What is your $26,900,000 railway going to do there? Going to take through traffic? What does the Minister of Railways say?-we cannot make the Intercolonial railway pay because we cannot hitch it on to the through traffic. But the way to make it pay is to establish a competing line and put $26,-
900,000	of the people's money into that competing line ! That is one way to make it pay. Would the trustee of an estate manage the estate in that way? I do not believe it and I do not believe that the people in this country- have yet got down into their minds the extravagant, aimless, unbusinesslike way in which this government that pretends to business management, has been carrying on the affairs of this country.
If the House will bear with me a minute more I would just like to touch the Grand Trunk Pacific, which is the last child of my right hon. friend and a boy whom he expects to grow up, live for ever, and bestow constant praises upon his parent. I think I do not hazard any statement that is extreme when I say that the manner in which the government went into the construction of this railway did not argue foresight, business management or common prudence. What engineering or other knowledge had they of a large portion of the route which they determined by drawing a line on the map was to be followed by that railway. In reference to the Quebec-Moncton section, what necessity in the world was there for putting $26,900,000 of money there instjead of 'faking $8,000,000 or $10,000,000 and putting "the present Intercolonial railway in a first-class position, quite sufficient to carry all the traffic that would follow in the wake of this development? But, if there is one thing more than another in which these trustees have failed in their duty to their stockholders it is in this that their information was so faulty that it deceived their stockholders. The chief trustee and his lieutenant the Finance Minister, came before this House and the fpeople of the country and declared that you could build that section of the road from Moncton to Winnipeg for $51,000,000, or a little more. Is there any doubt about that? When the Prime Minister was questioned as to how he knew that, what information he had, he said they had mountains of information and he pledged his word to the people that that was a fair calculation of the cost. I hove put some questions on the Order 48
Paper. I have, the result of those questions here from the Minister of Railways and Canals and they show that from Winnipeg t) Lake Superior Junction the total expenditure will be $20,984,690, that from Lake Superior Junction to Quebec, $66,473,171 is the estimated expenditure, of which twenty-seven and a third millions have been already spent. That makes $87,457,361 from Winnipeg to Quebec. Then from Quebec to Moncton the total cost, as given by the Minister of Railways and Canals, most of it spent, some estimated, is $26,935,902, which makes in all, $114,393,763, which is the latest estimate after half of the expenditure has been made, or may be a little more as the total cost of that portion of the line. Contrast that with your $51,000,000, which was estimated by the right hon. gentleman and by the Minister of Finance and put forward in circular form to the shareholders and stockholders and upon which circular information shareholders and stockholders voted them the power to carry out .the expenditure. Is that brilliant management? is it honest management ? I am talking about honesty in this way, that before a trustee or director will commit his stockholders to a large exnenditure he should regard it as his bounden duty to know the ground upon which he stands. Did these gentlemen know the ground upon which they stood, did they take any pains to find out the ground upon which they stood? Because they did not they mislead their shareholders and stockholders and I say it was not honest treatment in the true sense of the word which demands that before you draw your shareholders into an investment you must exhaust all proper measures for getting information upon which y-our plan is presented to them. Well, Sir, that is not all the cost. I am not going into the calculation of interest, but it strikes any one that the interest calculated by the Minister of Finance and adhered to by the Prime Minister on their small computation of the cost will be doubled and more than doubled on this actual fulfilment of the cost; so that you have to add probably three times as much for interest as you would have had to on the lesser computation of cost. Then you have the Quebec bridge, which has to be considered now as part of the line, and at least $14,000,000 will be necessary for that, which makes the cost of that connection from Winnipeg to Moncton $128,800,000. To this add several millions for terminals at Quebec and Winnipeg. I ask the business men of this country whether they consider that this is brilliant, businesslike administration? It would be sufficient in a company to have these directors succeeded quickly by others and I am not sure that it would not go even much farther than that. One thing I noticed when I was in the AVest, and it is this: There is a whole area of country up there



that they call the two-track country. What does it mean? The Prime Minister, when he advised his directors and shareholders to go into that project told them that this was to open up new territory, to use his own words at Winnipeg, it was to plunge into new territory: wdiat it really means is that from Winnipeg to Edmonton and, maybe some distance beyond, lines of railway cross and intercross for hundreds of mites and you never are practically out of sight of the Canadian Northern or the Canadian Pacific railway and in many cases you can drop a pea from your car window on to the track of the Canadian Pacific railway. There is an extensive country into which the farmers are rushing to use their brawn and their muscle to till the soil, and there are two railroads with elevators here and elevators across the street, a double set of railroads and a double set of elevators, and r:o competition notwithstanding that. What an outrageous thing it is that when that section of the country was absolutely provided for by lines of railway already running, or existing under charter and being built, that Canada should have spent millions upon millions of dollars in paralleling lines of transport which were already quite sufficient for the country through which they passed, to the neglect of other equally fertile country which is without a mile of railway. And to the latest day of Canadian history, as in a less degree no man will pass by the Newmarket canal without curling the lip of scorn, so Sir, there is one monument which is certain for all time to my right hon. friend-it is the fact, that when he had large power, and large confidence, and the people's money in his hand, in that great northwest which longs for new avenues of transportation in territory not served by railways, he had seen fit to parallel for 800 miles or more existing lines of railway. Is that business management? And, in view of all these things which I have mentioned and which are but one hundredth part of what one might mention, I put it to the House, and I put it to the people of the country, whether it is not time for a change?

We have had to-day the statement of the Finance Minister, from which we learn that the surplus that now may well be estimated for the present year is $16,500,000, that the expenditure has been reduced to the extent of as nearly as may be the same amount, that the addition to the public debt has been $17,500,000 and only that, notwithstanding that $20,000,000 have been expended this year on the Transcontinental railway. We have the statement of the Finance Minister to-day that the net public debt of Canada is now, not $50-82 as in 1896, but $45-85, a decrease per capita of Mr. FOSTER.
$4-97. That, Sir, is a most satisfactory statement, it is a statement upon which we may well congratulate the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the cabinet, who are indeed a trust company, who realize that they are, as the member for North Toronto has said, a trust company; not a Union Trust Company, but a real honest, well managed trust company having at heart the good of the people they represent. 1 say, Sir, that the people of this country will offer their congratulations to the Minister of Finance to-day, and it is not the first time he has deserved congratulation. He has gotten into the habit of offering to us, year by year, such welcome financial statements as we have just heard from him. When I say that he has acquired the habit of giving us such financial statements, it reminds me of one of Harry Lauder's popular songs in which the singer represents himself as going home to his good wife under the influence of too much Mountain Dew, and the wife began to upraid and scold him, and she said: ' Mon, its gettin to be a habit wi ye;' and the reply was: ' Na, its no a habit, its a gif.' And so I say that with the Finance Minister these prosperous budget speeches are not so much a habit as a gift. Not only has the Minister of Finance the gift of presenting such statements, but he has the much higher gift of so regulating and conducting the financial affairs of Canada as to bring about and maintain the conditions which make it possible for him to deliver such a statement, year after year. The member for North Toronto has endeavoured to assail that statement, to detract from its value and to lessen its influence upon the people of Canada.' The member for North Toronto is clever. With all the cunning 'of an Indian juggler, with all the keen imagination of a poet, with all the inventiveness of the author of Gulliver's Travels, with the ability to paint words as none other but he can, he has endeavoured to detract from that financial statement and trom its true value. But facts are stubborn things, and the facts which the Minister of Finance has given us to-day cannot be controverted and their influence cannot be lessened in the mind of the people even by the remarks of such as the member for North Toronto. The words of that hon. gentleman have fallen harmless as the smallest sized bird shot as we hear it pattering down from the rocky walls of an impregnable fortress or from the impregnable sides of an ironclad; his words have made as little impression as the clapping of the desks by the ever too ready auditors who sit behind him. I was much interested in the speech which was delivered by the hon. member (Mr. Foster) to-night. I heard it last year I heard it again this year; it is indeed becoming familiar. In his remarks last year the hon. member (Mr. Foster) was exceedingly

sarcastic and he accused the Minister of Fnance of lacking in boldness and courage. I quote from ' Hansard ' of the 20th of April last:
He (Mr. Fielding) is hopeful. He gives a wonderfully precise forecast for that year. Here we are already in the year 1909-10 and yet the only forecast the Minister of Finance can give us is that he hopes there will he a reasonable percentage of increase in the revenue over that of last year, while with reference to the expenditure he did not even hazard a guess as to what it would be. Former Ministers of Finance have been a little more daring than that; they have at least, when they -were near the end of a year, made what they considered a forecast of both revenue and expenditure and they put their forecast to the test.
The .hon. member (Mr. Foster) in these words accuses the Minister of Finance of a lack of daring. Well, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is an exceedingly irodest man considering the long series of successes he has had; he is not given to boasting even of what he has done, let alone what he expects to do; he is not given to hazarding wide guesses. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has well said that former Finance Ministers have been a little more daring. We know, Sir, you and I know, >the people of this country know, at least one former Finance Minister who. w'as much more daring in the way of prophesy and hazarding guesses. He loomed up large as a lion when making
prophesy at the beginning of the year, but at the end of the year when he was explaining why the prophesies had not been fulfilled he became rather of the size and the gentle disposition of the household kitten. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) speaking again last year said:
It would have seemed befitting in a Finance Minister who was careful and prudent to have made his provision when the danger was coming, to have drawn his sail when the storm was about to burst.
I do not blame the hon. member for having been rather mistaken in his guess last year. I do not blame him under the circumstances for seeing signs of a storm, but what does seem strange is that this year he should have repeated the word and have alluded to a storm. Wild fancies as to what may happen are one thing, and halucinations that possess a man as to what has happened are quite another thing. The storm about to burst? Where, Sir, has been the storm? Where on the ocean of Canadian finance has there been any great troubling of the waters, and has it not all been a tempest, in the little brain of the hon. member for North Toronto? Storm, Sir! Where has there been the snapping or the breaking of a mast? Where has there been the rending of a 48i
single sail, the loss of a single anchor? Not a man overboard, not an ounce of cargo lost, the sea to-day as smooth as glass, the sun shining brightly and hot a cloud in the financial or commercial sky of Canada.
Talking about finances, I find that the public debt of the United States at the end of 1907 was $878,596,755 and at the end of 1908 it had increased to $938,132,409, an increase in one year of over fifty-nine and a half million dollars. That was at the end of 1908. What progress is being made in the United States to-day? I read this article from the 'Weekly Times' of London, of November 5, an extract from a letter written by their Washington correspondent :
Two and a half months ago the Payne tariff came into effect, hut already it is clear that the new rates will fall far short of extinguishing the deficit for the current fiscal year. From the beginning of the year-July 1-to October 27 the deficit on ordinary expenditures and disbursements amounts to .$26,000,000, a reduction of only $13,000,000 on the unusual deficit for the same period last year, although it must he remembered that the Payne law came into effect only on August 5, and that the minimum rates under the special treaties continues in -force. The customs receipts have been increasing, but ordinary disbursements are also increasing. For the current year up to October 27 the disbursements were $241,425,000 against $227,702,000 for the same period last year. Moreover, the customs receipts are expected to show a decline next month. As the working balance of the treasury is only $27,000,000, a prolongation of the deficit is expected soon to compel a recourse to a loan to meet current expenses.
So that in that great republic to the south of us, having an area not larger than ours, having a population ten times as great as ours, having had large capital and a population of the same blood as ours to develop their resources, even at this-day they have to make a loan to meet current expenses.
I think it is a matter of congratulation that we have received the statement we have heard to-day. The hon. member for North Toronto says that last year in place of having a surplus of a little over $1,000,000, if the bounties had been charged to revenue there would not have been a surplus but a small deficit. This the Finance Minister frankly pointed out and stated in his address. The hon. member for North Toronto contends that these bounties ought to be charged to revenue, although the Finance Minister has well and logically argued that if subsidies to railways aie properly chargeable to capital account, as they have always been under this government and the preceding government, upon the same principle these bounties ought to be charged to the same account. I do

think myself, and I say frankly, that it would be better if both railway subsidies and .bounties were charged to revenue account. But I want to know whether if the system of bookkeeping were changed in that respect our friends on the other side of the House and their supporters would be frank enough, would be honest enough to explain the difference in the method of bookkeeping to their electors as they went among them during a campaign. I doubt if they would.
Almost tragically the hon. member for North Toronto savs: What has saved the Finance Minister? The Finance Minister has not been in any very particular danger. What has saved the country? Neither has the country been in any great danger since 1896. But listen to the reply of the hon. member for North Toronto to his own question. He says that the farmers have saved the Finance Minister and have saved the country. To a large extent he is perfectly right, to a large extent the farmers have saved the country. But they do not deserve all the credit; the sailors, the fishermen, the miners, the lumbermen, the factory hands, all deserve some share of the credit, and were it not for the farmers and these other men who toil we would not have, admittedly, the country we have to-day. The hon. member, and this is a renetition of the old story, has asked over and over again who purchased and opened up the great Northwest? We admit that the northwestern country was purchased by a Conservative government. We admit that during the regime of the Conservative party the Canadian Pacific railway was run through that northwest country to open it up. We give them all the credit to which they are entitled for the purchase they made of that northwestern country, and we give them such credit as they are entitled to for the building of the Canadian Pacific railway. We are told, they were told, at the time they were undertaking the building of that road, that it could be built more cheaply, that other people were willing to build it at that very time at a lower price, at a less cost, and [DOT]without the villainous arrangement as to taxation that was coupled with the bargain they made. They took the dearer rather than the cheaper bargain, and we hove been paying for it ever since, and as far as taxation is concerned will pay for it, I suppose, while the world lasts. Yet they are entitled to a degree of credit. Sir, who put the farmers in that country? Our friends opposite purchased the country and then left it lying almost a waste. To whom is due the credit of developing that country? I claim that this government deserves the credit for putting into that great western country the very farmers of whom the hon. member spoke to-Mr. MILLER.
night, I think I can prove it by his own words. Talking of the Yukon he says: When you went to the Yukon you found
38,000	people there; to-day you have a population of 5,000-and he blamed the government. Sir, if the government are to blame because the population of the Yukon is less to-day than it was, then on the same reasoning they are entitled to credit because the population of the Northwest has increased so greatly. But he says the farmer who grew the grain, who saved the country, has to pay a great deal more for the clothes he wears, for the lumber he buys, for the labour he employs.
Now, let us take the hon. gentleman for once at his word. The farmers have to pay more for the clothes they wear; what does the manufacturer of the clothes say to that-does he object? The farmer has to pay more for the lumber he buys; does the sawmiller object? The farmer has to pay more for the labour he employs; does the labourer object? Accepting the argument of the hon. gentleman, that this government is to blame for increasing the prices the farmer has to pay, by this very act this government has enabled the manufacturer of clothing and the manufacturer of lumber to get better prices for the goods they sell, and has enabled the farm labourer to get better wages. What kind of a man does the hon. member for North Toronto think the Canadian farmer is? How hig does he think is the heart of the average Canadian farmer? The Canadian farmer-the hon. member for North Toronto will not, I am sure, deny it-is receiving to-day larger prices for his horses, his cattle, his hogs, his wheat, and his dairy products, than the farmers of this country ever received before, since Columbus discovered America. The farmer is able to pay higher prices for the goods he buys, and is able to pay a reasonable wage, as in the old Tory days he never was able to do. And the Canadian farmer is not only able to pay higher wages, but is large hearted enough to be willing to pay them to the man who helps him in his work. What is the government doing for the farmers who have been taken into that country? It has provided transportation; it has surveyed the lands of the northwest; it has provided post offices and mail routes; it is helping to develop the mines and minerals of the country; it is attempting to preserve the forests and to practice reforestation; it has established experimental farms. This government has not only taken the farmers into that country but is providing for them while they are there.
The next question the hon. gentleman raised was the balance of trade between this country and the United States. In his conclusion he forgot and omitted one important item, that is, the $60,000,000 of cold

cash that American farmers alone have taken into that western country during the last seven months, and he has forgotten the probably $60,000,000 more in farm stock and household goods which they have taken with them.
The hon. gentleman next advised the government not to tie their hands, in order that they might be able, when the time comes, if it does come, to accept a preference at the hands of the mother country. If this was given as a word of caution and advice, we take it in the spirit in which it was given. If it was rebuke, it was one that we were not entitled to, because one of the conditions of the French treaty is that it may be cancelled at any time upon twelve months' notice.
The hon. gentleman endeavoured to make a point against the Finance Ministei because the government of Canada is paying to-day a higher rate of interest than it paid some years ago. That is no evidence of carelessness or bad financing for the price of money and the rate of interest rises and falls as does the price of wheat. If the hon. member could prove, as he did not attempt to prove, that Canada is paying to-day a higher rate of interest than other countries similarlv situated, he would have, made out his case.
The hon. gentleman next accused the govenment of wasting money because of the payment of underwriters for underwriting government loans. As to that. I quote from the Colonial Office journal, published in England, for July of the present year. The editors of that journal, who are well acquainted with the various systems of finance, say:
It is the practice now-a-days on the issue of colonial loans and others of a like kind to get them underwritten. The underwriters, in consideration of a commission, which is usually 1 per cent, undertake to take so much of the loan as is not subscribed for by the public. Governments would, of course, not sacrifice 1 per cent, if they could get money without employing underwriters, but experience has shown that on the whole they gain by doing so. Only a very small part of a loan is applied for by the real public at the time of issue. The ordinary investor buys stocks and shares at a moment when he has money available, which is not often; it is the professional who examines the morning newspaper and makes use of the few hours, which are often all that is allowed, to come to a decision and send in his application. If the issue is readily taken up so that the price is likely to go to a premium, the list must be closed early, as otherwise on the news getting about a vast number of applications would be sent in with the object of getting advantage of the premium, and this would be unfair to the genuine applicants. The result is that the success depends practically on the view which the market takes of the deal, and this is largely a matter of the influence of the financial houses interested.
So that upon this high authority we find that the system now in vogue by all governments requiring to borrow is that of the employment of underwriters, as has been done by the hon. Minister of Finance.
The hon. member for North Toronto complained that we are not in this country creating a sinking fund to meet our maturing loans, as is done in England. If it were possible to have such a sinking fund, I would be very glad, but it is not fair to argue that Canada, a new and undeveloped country of large extent, has the saVne opportunity to create a sinking fund that is possible in an old, well developed, wealthy country of small area like Great Britain
The hon. member next sang the old song about this government taking more in taxation from the people of Canada than the preceding government did, saying that this government took $11 a head while the old government had taken only $5.50. The hon. member has already stated that this government has raised the wages of workingmen and the prices received by manufacturers. And in that he is quite correct; a workman to-day is just as easily able to obtain $1.50 per day of wages as under the old Conservative rule, he was able to obtain $1 a day. Therefore, he receives-the hon. member said because of the action of this government-about $150 more in wages in a year than he did under the old regime. And he has to pay $5.50 more according to the hon. member in yearly taxation. Well, he has made a fairly good bargain; he has made about $144.50 through having this government in power instead of continuing the old government. It is an old argument, one that has often been made and will often he made again, that this government takes more in taxation out of the people than the other government did. But the hon. member (Mr. Foster) admits-he did not admit it cheerfully but merely because he had to, nor did he admit it to the extent that the facts justify-that this government, leaving out the question of bounties, is exacting a lower rate of duty than the former government did. If a man to-day goes to any store to make a purchase, he finds that the goods have been subject to a lower duty than the same goods under a former government. And, Sir, does this government compel any man to buy two coats where formerly he bought only one or to buy two pair of shoes where formerly he bought only one? But, because as the hon. member has stated, that man receives higher wages and so is able to buy his wife a dress that, in the old days, he could not think of buying, or is able to buy a suit of clothes for himself more than he formerly bought, he, by that transaction, voluntarily contributes more largely to the revenue of the country.

I have said that the hon. member (Mr. Foster) delivered much the same speech to-night as he did a year ago. He used one argument exactly the same as that he gave-last year. In calculating the increase of the debt under the Conservative party from 1878 to 1896, he said we ought to deduct from the total the price of 7,500,000 acres of land that they got back from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Now, I am perfectly willing to allow the hon. gentleman that credit. He has given us to-night the same argument exactly that he did a year ago, with the exception, that a year ago he began that part of his speech by saying that the Conservative party from 1886 to 1896 increased the public debt by $35,000,000: to-night he says that from 1879 to 1896 they increased the public debt by $118,000,000, otherwise, the speeches were the same. His argument being the same, let me read to the House the argument I then made in reply: I quote from last year's ' Hansard ':
The hon. member for North Toronto admitted that the Conservative party in ten years from 1886 to 1896 had increased the public debt by $35,000,000. But then he argued that while they had increased the public debt by $35,000,000, for $10,000,000 of that they had received 7,500,000 acres of land, and he said if that 7,500,000 acres be worth $3 an acre, it makes a total of $22,000,000 to be deducted from the $35,000,000 by which they had increased the debt.
I say I am perfectly willing to admit that, But let me go further:
But he maintained that the land was worth more than $3 an acre, he said: ' If you calculate its value at $6 an acre, it makes $45,000,000 which will exceed the whole addition to the public debt.'
I am willing to admit that also.
I am perfectly willing that the hon. member should make that argument, I am perfectly willing to accept his figures and his statement, hut I would ask him, were he here, where the lands came from that they purchased for $10,000,000. He would state that the 7,500,000 acres was part of 25,000,000 acres that the Conservative government had given to the Canadian Pacific railway for nothing at all. I would say to him: I am perfectly willing that you should give your party credit at $6 an acre for the 7,500,000 acres you thus obtained, but if I do you must be willing to he charged at the same rate with the 46,000,000 acres that your government gave away while in power to persons other than actual settlers, and so while I credit you with $42,000,000, I charge you with $276,000,000, and I do not think the hon. member would make the account look any better for his party.
I said then, Sir, that, on his own reasoning, I would charge his party with 46,000,000 acres of land making a total of $276,000,000; but, Sir, the price of land has gone up. To-night, the hon. gentleman fixes the price at $8 per acre. On that basis, Mr. MILLER.
I should have to charge him for the 46,000,000 acres $368,000,000. Now, I suppose, if the hon. member lives for another twenty years-and I hope he will, for he is, I think, the greatest asset that we on this side of the House have-he will come to charge us for that 7,500,000 acres of land, I suppose $50 an acre. If he does, on his own reasoning, I shall have a very large account indeed to charge to the Conservative party.
The hon. member next-I think I am not unparliamentary when I say-had the nerve to talk about the land that this government had given away to parties other than actual settlers. I might have expected that Irom some body else who did not know any better, who did not know the history of the Conservative party and what they had been guilty of, but I hardly expected it to come now from the hon. member from North Toronto. Why? Because, in the eighteen years that they were in office, his government gave away land to persons other than actual settlers representing a total of 46,000,000 acres, and at the same time they gave to the actual settler only 7,900,000 acres, or a little more than we have given to the actual settler in the first seven months of the present year. The hon. member next spoke of the investigation that took place in the Marine and Fisheries Department. That too is an old story, often repeated and often to be repeated no doubt. He told of the iniquity and corruption that had been discovered by the investigating commission. It is true the commission said there was corruption in connection with the Marine Department. They said there had been corruption in connection with the Marine Department ever since confederation and for every one of the three hundred and sixty-five days of every one of the eighteen long years during which the Conservative party had been in power.
So they are growing worse.

My hon. friend has not read the report or he would not say that. But the commissioners did give the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries credit for making an honest effort to improve the condition of affairs in his department, a credit which these gentlemen did not give to any minister who had preceded him. The hon. gentleman said they wanted to go into all the departments and they were not permitted. Sir, we have a Public Accounts Committee before which any charge can be taken and investigated. What has been the custom of our friends on the other side? To make a charge, and they always took care that it was a serious charge, they always took care to make it loudly, they always took care to advertise it all over Canada as soon as they had made it, and

before it had been investigated; but when the Public Accounts Committee met and they had an opportunity to investigate their charges they had so wrongly made and so wrongly circulated before they were investigated, when I say they were given an opportunity to investigate, they had other business, oftentimes they did not even attend the sittings of the committee, they threw up their hands, and said in effect that they had accomplished all their purpose when they made their charges and got them in the newspapers.
The hon. member then speaks of a certain' place where some $40,000 has been spent in dredging for the accommodation of one launch and one little steamer, and that, he said, was a piece of political rascality, of political iniquity. Sir, I do not know that we can come hastily to that conclusion. If there is a place where any considerable number of people live, they may be humble people, they may not have much political influence, they may be poor fisher folk, they may be poor tillers of the soil, but if that one steamer and that one launch is the only means they have of getting to market, or of communicating with the outside world, then I say that that expenditure is justified. This is a government that has spent a great deal of money in endeavouring to benefit every class of people, those who till the soil, those who go to sea in their fishing boats, and those who dig minerals in the mines.
I suppose we will not for a long time hear the last of the Quebec bridge. Now what are the facts? The Quebec bridge was built, and the Quebec bridge fell down. The Quebec bridge was built according to plans and specifications that were drawn up by men who were recognized and generally admitted to be the best bridge building engineers on the American continent, or in the world. The engineers who drew the plans and who drew the specifications for the Quebec bridge, were recommended to this government by whom? By Mr. Schrei-ber, the government engineer, a gentleman who was the faithful employee of the Conservative government by whom he was appointed, and who has continued, I believe, to be the faithful employee of this government. When that bridge collapsed, what did the world say, what did the engineering world say? They said: This is a matter of great concern to us, this is a matter of great concern to every man in the engineering profession. That bridge, they said, was planned by men that we believed to be experts, by men whom we believed to be the very best bridge engineers in the world, and if that bridge, built according to their plans and specifications, has collapsed, it simply means this, that that gigantic bridge, a very long bridge, much longer than most of the bridges that had hitherto
been built, was wrongly designed, why, it means that our whole theory of bridge building is at fault, our engineers are wrong, we will have to revise our plans and adopt new methods. No blame, Sir, can be attached, and no blame will be attached by men who are acquainted with the facts, to this government for the misfortune which befell the Quebec bridge. Such charges as that are only made in the absence of any real and true grounds of complaint.
The Newmarket canal is characterized as the Aylesworth ditch. I am sorry the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is not in his seat. We used to know that as the Newmarket canal. Upon a certain occasion the member for York, the present hoA. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) gave the hon. member for North Toronto perhaps the greatest castigation ever received by any man in this House, and ever since then this canal has been known as the Aylesworth ditch. It is not a public work of any less value because you call it by any such name as that, it does not lessen the importance of the work. Now, Sir, there was vigorous cheering, there was vigorous desk pounding to-day, when the hon. member mentioned the Newmarket canal. Sir, I venture to say that not one man in twenty of those who sit behind the hon. member and who cheered him, ever saw that canal or know a single thing about it. I talked to a man to-day who was telling me, and I am sure honestly, what he thought. He said that that Newmarket canal would be of very great advantage to the section through which it runs. For my part I >do not know anything about it. I say frankly, Sir, that I am just as ignorant of the Newmarket canal, of its method of construction, of the country through which it runs, or the way in which it will answer the purpose for which it is intended, as the majority of the members who applauded my hon. friend.
Then the building of the St. Andrew's lock was criticised. I do not know anything about the St. Andrew's lock except what I have been told. And I wonder how many members on the other side of the House know anything about the St. Andrew's lock. But I am told by a man who knows much more about it than the hon. member for North Toronto, that the building of the St. Andrew's lock opens up to the city of Winnipeg 350 miles of waterway.
Sir, when in the most harrowing terms, the member for North Toronto was picturing some of the sins and iniquities of this government, I almost felt like believing him for a moment. I do not often feel that way when he goes on a tirade of that kind. But when he mentioned the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, and found the fault he did, I said: Well, any intelligent man who would tell that story over again and

endeavour to get this House or the people to take any stock in it, is scarcely entitled to any credence. There was one member, the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) who, I noticed, although a close political friend of the member for Toronto, did not applaud very vigorously when the Sas-katchewtn Valley Land Company was mentioned. What are the facts, recounting them briefly? Nobody regarded that part of the country given to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company as being of any value. My hon. friend from West Toronto considered it to be of no value, and would not [DOT] accept it as 'part of a land grant to which his company was entitled. The government sold the land to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, and on what conditions. They said: We will sell you this land at a very low price per acre, hut only on condition that you will place settlers upon it, a certain definite numoer per township, on the lands that we so sell to you. Now, Sir, we are giving away lands in the west for nothing to people who will come and settle upon them. The hon. member for West Toronto was one of the chief stockholders in the railway that ran through that tract of land, and I understand that for a stretch of sixty miles there was no railway station on that line. Why? Because the owners of the railway said: Nobody can cultivate that soil with any profit, nobody will settle upon it, it will never yield a crop, and it would not pay us to put a railway station there. When they were pressed to do so by the Saskatchewan Land Company they said: We will, cn condition that you pay the salary of our station agent; and only by that means was a railway station established. With what success did the government endeavour to settle that country? With this degree of success that they brought into that country, at very great expense and with the exercise of a giept deal of energy, people who understood how to till and cultivate such soil. With what result? The hon. member for North Toronto admits that to-day that country blossoms like the rose, that to-day that country, once a barren district in which i.obody had any confidence, is now one of the most fertile parts of the northwest; and, Sir, that it is admitted generally by the people of the west that one of the very best and most enterprising acts of this government, one of the acts of this government attended with the very best results, was the sale of that land upon the terms upon which it was sold to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company. We have it upon the evidence of the hon. member for North Toronto that it is,now good land, that it is now fertile and productive, and I say, Sir, that the hon. member for North Toronto is no mean judge of northwest land, because in his day he has bought and sold north-Mr. MILLER.
west land to a large extent. The people in that neighbourhood, knowing the history of that transaction, knowing the land and knowing what has been made of the land, have sent to this House members to support, not the party of the hon. member for North Toronto, but the party that is sitting behind the Premier and the Minister of Finance to-day.
The hon. member for North Toronto made some tart remarks about the Intercolonial railway. I will not say anything in defence of the Intercolonial railway tonight, because, in the first place, I do not think it is necessary and because, in the second place, I believe that before very long the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) will present a report to this House that will be as displeasing and as discouraging to the hon. member of North Toronto as it will be satisfactory and pleasing to the people of this country. I recommend the hon. member for North Toronto to go to the library, take down 'Hansard' and read from a debate that took place in this House some years ago respecting the Intercolonial railway in which he will find the words of his former leader, Sir Charles Tupper, to the effect that the Intercolonial was never intended to be a paying road and was never expected to be.
Now, I want very shortly to speak of some of the things that have been and are being done by the several departments of this government, or, at least, by one or two of them for the benefit of the people of Canada. I want to speak for a moment of the forestry work that is being prosecuted by the Department of the Interior. The Forestry branch was established in 1899. The first appropriation that this government made for the work was in the years 1900-1 and the appropriation in that year was $10,000. That appropriation has grown from year to year until last year and the year before the appropriation was $100,000. In this forestry work the department employs a staff of about forty people. In the United States, for carrying on the same kind of work, they employ permanently a staff of about 2,000 people and their annual appropriation has risen until at this date it is $4,640,000. The forestry branch is endeavouring to ascertain the extent of the forest wealth of our country, and it is preserving the forest from fire through the efforts of the fire rangers and by enlisting, through the missionaries of the country, the sympathies of the Indians. They are also assisting in the reforestation of the western country, and in the reforestry of the western country there are difficulties to be met with that are not known to us in the east; in the first place, the comparatively light rainfall, in the second place, the exposure of young trees to great winds and storms, and in the third place, the

compactness and hardness of the soil. Notwithstanding these difficulties the department last year gave away to 2,010 applicants, 2,570,000 trees for planting. The applications for this year are largely in excess of those of last year, and from the time of the founding of this forestry branch 14,500,000 trees have been given away free to settlers of the west for planting upon western plains. I call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the changes in the regulations for the sale of timber as made in the month of December, 1907. By these new regulations it is enacted, first, that every sale of government timber shall be by auction, second, that there shall be a cruising and survey of every limit before it is put up for sale and, in the third place, that there shall be the fixing of an upset price. The form of the timber license provides that the licensee, first, shall not cut trees less than ten inches in diameter at the stump; second, shall leave seed trees as directed by the forestry officers; and third, shall dispose of the debris as instructed.
Now, let me sav a word as to the iron and steel bounties. It was, last summer, my privilege and pleasure to visit Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I confess that I had not been particularly in love with the payment of bounties. The iron and steel bounties have averaged, I believe, a little over $1,000,000 a year for the time this government has been in power, making about 15 or 16 cents for each person in Canada per annum. When in Nova Scotia I availed myself of the opportunity of seeing large iron and steel works in different parts of the province. I had the opportunity of going through one of the large works, conducted by a director of the company, and when I saw the works in operation, and when I saw the effect of the works, I will readily admit that I was glad that this government had encouraged the iron and steel industries by the payment of bounties. I realized that the men who, at great risk, had put a wealth of capital and a wealth of intelligence and enterprise into those great industries were indeed helping to a considerable degree in the building up of the nation. I realized that the lusty workmen in these factories, who were pouring the molten metal, who were shaping large masses of iron under steam hammers, who were rolling it into greater lengths and turning it in their great lathes were assisting to utilize and develop the natural resources that a generous Creator had placed upon, under and convenient to Canadian soil intending them to be used for and by the Canadian people. As I saw large thriving towns and growing cities that had before the establishment of these industries been sleepy villages, fishing hamlets and market centres for
the small surrounding district of farming country I realized that a great deal had been done by the building up of these industries. As I saw these workmen engaged in large numbers in these works it occurred to me, as it would to any one, that these men must be fed and clothed, that these men were buying the boots and shoes, the cottons and woollens that were being made at the benches and upon the looms of other Canadian factories. I realized that these workmen must be fed from the product of Canadian farms and Canadian pastures, and I realized too that these workmen buying that which they had to buy and these manufacturers importing that which they had to import must be adding largely to the customs revenue of the country. Pei'haps I was influenced a little bit in looking favourably upon the iron and steel bounties by words that had been uttered by the hon. member for North Toronto and which I read in the 'Hansard' of 1894. The hon. gentleman said:
On the one hand the duties on iron have been and are relatively high, on the other hand there is the patent fact that unless there be a sufficient inducement in the way of protection or bounty given for the manufacture of iron it will be impossible in this country as it has been found impossible in all other countries ever to rise from the production of raw ores which abound in this country, to an independent and self contained manufacture of the larger portion of the iron needed for the consumption of the country.
I possibly have been influenced to some extent by these words of the hon. member (Mr. Poster) and Sir, while I was glad that the iron and steel bounties had been paid, when I saw recently in the newspapers that one of these companies whose works I had seen had declared a stockj bonus of 20 per cent, and when I read the words of the general manager of one of these companies which I shall quote, I came to the conclusion that the time had now come when the iron and steel bounties ought no longer to be paid. Sir, I do not want the people of this country to be prejudiced, I do not want the people of this country to too hastily draw conclusions because of the payment of a 20 per cent stock bonus, I want it to be understood that this 20 per cent stock bonus was in the place of annual dividends which had been withheld and not paid. But notwithstanding that the stock bonus was only the equivalent for honestly earned reasonable dividends yet when I read the words of Mr. Cantley, the general manager of the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, I came to the conclusion which I have already referred to. Referring to his company Mr. Cantley said:
It is already in an unusually advantageous

position having its own iron ore and the coal and being in no way dependent upon any other concern. The company's output of coal was larger than ever this year and the deposit both of coal and iron ore at Wabana are practicallv inexhaustible. Everything in connection with our property is encouraging and with the improvements in finances the company can go ahead and work out its own destiny to greater advantage than if it were in a merger.
I take these words from the ' Monetary Times ' of December 4, 1909, which publishes the annual address of the general manager at the last meeting of this company. Now, Sir, the Nova Scotia Iron and Steel Company are not, I fancy, in any different position than the other iron and steel companies of the Dominion. I think the language used by Mr. Cantley is language that no man need be ashamed of; it is the language of a man who has self reliance and self dependence. I believe that a man who at the annual meeting of this company can say: 'We are now in a position to work our own destiny independent of any merger ' will be willing to say: ' We are now in a position to work out our own destiny without any iron or steel bounties from any government.' And Sir, I trust when the term expires, as it will expire next year, for the payment of iron and steel bounties that it will not be renewed. Unless I change my mind more than I think I will, I shall be utterly opposed to their renewal.
We have made a treaty recently with France. As to the commercial advantages to be derived from that treaty I will say but little because it is a matter that has been already fully discussed. There is one thing I do wish to say to the farmers of this country, and when I say it I am simply repeating what has been stated by the ' Farm Journal ' published at Winnipeg. That journal has referred to the considerable benefit which will accrue to the farmers of Canada from the negotiations of the French treaty, and it does not speak of it in terms of praise because of the advantages for the shipment of stockers or fat cattle, but it says that the manufacturers of agricultural implements in Canada will be so largely helped by that French treaty, and their trade will be so increased and extended that they will put up much larger factories with greater capacity, giving a greater output, and that having that increased capacity and output, as a consequence the price of agricultural implements all over Canada will be largely decreased.
But, Sir, it is not so important because of the trade advantages that are likely to accrue, although there will be trade advantages, but it is because we always receive an indirect benefit when we make a trade treaty with any other nation in as much that we get their friendship. And if Mr. MILLER.
we suffer no material loss I think it _ is worth while to make such a treaty with jur neighbours whomsoever they may be even if the only good result to us is the good will of the persons with whom we treat. Sir, we have made a treaty with France; I trust that when that treaty has been gotten well out of the way that this government will be willing to embrace the first opportunity of making a treaty with Germany. I believe we will derive advantages from the French treaty, but I also believe that our advantages would be still greater from a German treaty; greater because Germany is not such a great agricultural nation as France, that it is more of a manufacturing nation, that it will consume more of our products. In that respect a reasonable trade treaty with Germany would help us even to greater advantage than a treaty with France. Sir, I am not in any way blaming the government, there certainly can be no blame attached to it, for the imposition of the Ger-' man surtax. There was nothing else for them to do under the circumstances. But if Germany is now willing, as we are told she is, to approach this government in a friendly way and ask for closer trade relations, I trust the Canadian government will not be reluctant to meet them. When we were discussing the French treaty one gentleman on the other side of the House objected because of a knitted goods factory at some place, and another lion, gentleman opposite objected because of a glove factory at some other place. Sir, if we are to regard ourselves as nation builders, if we are to regard ourselves as trustees having the development of a great country in our charge, we must look at these matters from a broader point of view. Such views may be all right to be held by members of a municipal council if the area of the municipality is not too great, but these are not the views that ought to be entertained by nation builders.
In considering a proposed German treaty and the conditions existing as between Germany and Canada I desire to make some reference to an article in the ' Empire Review ' for November, 1909, edited by Sir Clement Kinloch-Cooke. After explaining and describing the conditions as they are to-day between Germany and Canada, the editor says:
There can be no doubt that the trade between the two countries has materially suffered by the altered conditions, and in the best interests of Canada it is unfortunate that the tariff committee of the association of Canadian manufacturers have reported against the remission of the surtax on German manufactures. Obviously the line for Germany to take is to withdraw the reprisals and then for Canada to withdraw the surtax. If this were done the position would revert automatically to the status quo. It appears Germany is willing to do her part but the tariff

committee do not see their way to accept the olive branch, giving as their reasons,-
Now follows, in quotation marks, the resolution of the Tariff Committee of the Manufacturers' association:
that the feeling amongst Canadian manufacturers against the negotiation of a tariff treaty with Germany has of late been strengthened by reason of the strong anti-German sentiment manifested in England and that from an imperial point of view it would certainly he unfortunate if at this juncture Canada were to strengthen the hands of Britain's most dreaded commercial rival by granting concessions which would be the means of transferring to that rival trade which is now being enjoyed by the mother country.
The comment of the editor is as follows:
But unsound as the commercial side of their policy is, the reference to ' the strong anti-German sentiment manifested in England ' is still more unsound. There is no strong anti-German feeling here in the sense that is implied in the tariff committee's report. A section of the press and of the public are, it is true, still opposed to all things German, hut the opposition politically is fast dying out. Commercial antagonism there must always be, but if Canada is to wait until all commercial jealously disappears before coming to terms with Germany she will postpone her arrangement till the Greek Kalends. If I might offer a suggestion to the Canadian government, it is this: ' Agree with your adversary quickly,' and leave all question of anti-German sentiment in this country out of your calculations.
We are now an important and a somewhat influential part of the British empire and I suggest that this government, not in any undignified way, but in a thoroughly business way, let it be known to Germany that we prefer trade rather than battles. If we do that I think it may have some influence in continuing peace rather than in bringing war. When we speak of a trade treaty with Germany, our friends on the other side of the House will say, as they said of the French treaty: What will the United States say. Sir, I was surprised to find our friends on the other side of the House ask such a question as that. I remember reading of men who were sent many long centuries ago to investigate a situation and to report, and on their return they said:
And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
If our friends on the other side are bound that before they make any bargain with any nation, they must obtain the censent of the people and government of the United States, then I say to them that so long as a people regard themselves as grasshoppers in their own sight they will be sure to be regarded as grasshoppers in the sight of the other fellow.
One thing more and I have done, and that is to refer shortly to the question of immigration. I shall not quote long figures, not even the figures I have prepared. I shall not s'peak so much as to the number of immigrants coming into the country just now, but rather as to the character of the immigrants we have received. I observe, Sir, that last year and for the first seven months of this year-and I think there is no change in that respect from the years preceding-more that seventy-five per cent of the immigrants we have received in Canada have been from Great Britain, Ireland and the United States. A large number of the remainder of the immigrants who have come here have been from the northern portion of Europe, from Germany, Sweden, Norway, Holland, and other portions of northern Europe, whose people are as good a class of immigrants as can be got to come to any country. I have said that the immigrants who have gone into the United States have been of an altogether different and inferior class. I say this because we have repeatedly heard it argued in this House that the United States have been getting a better class of immigrants than we in Canada because of the greater care that has been exercised by the people of the United States in the selection of their immigrants.
I wish to read shortly from an article in the * Popular Science ' Monthly ' by Dr. Albert Alleman, of Washington, District of Columbia. He says:
The people of the 13 colonies, the builders of the American union were almost exclusively of the Anglo-Saxon race. The immigration which set in after the war of independence and continued during the greater part of the nineteenth century, was composed of people not dissimilar from those early colonists. They came from the British Isles, Scandinavia, Germany and the smaller Teutonic countries. But during the last twenty-five years the number of immigrants from those regions has steadily decreased and has now sunk to very small numbers, while the immigration from Italy, Hungary, Greece and Russia has increased from year to year during the same period of time, and, of late years, lias assumed truly enormous proportions.
Again in the same article, he says:
Broadly speaking we have two great classes of immigrants, those that came before about the year 1885 and those that came after that year. The native home of the former was northwestern Europe and the bulk of them belongs to the so-called Teutonic, or Scandinavian, or the northern blonde race; the latter came from the Mediterranean basin and eastern Europe, and present a number of racial types.
Later in the same article, he says:
About the middle of the ninth decade of the last century,-
That would be about 1885.
-an entirely new immigration began to set in. The new arrivals came from southern and

eastern Europe, from Italy, Greece, Hungary, Bohemia, Eussia. Hailing from an entirely different region of Europe, they (lifter completely in their racial characteristics from the earlier immigration.
Here is sufficient evidence that Canada in the last twenty-five years has been receiving a class of immigrants vastly superior in every way to the immigrants who have, in the same time, been going into the United States.
A word as to the immigration from Japan. We all remember the great turmoil that was raised in this House and out of it a couple of years ago because of the great influx of Japanese immigrants. At the last election, in a certain section of this country, people were stampeded against the government of the day because of the fear of a yellow peril, which fear has since been shown to be purely without reason. The number of immigrants coming from Japan into Canada in 1907-8 was 7,601; in 1908-9, it was 495; and for the first seven months of 1909-10, only 186. It will therefore be seen that the fears of the people who were influenced to vote against this government in the last election because of the Japanese immigration and the failure of this government to stop it, were entirely groundless and these people will surely have learned the lesson that they had better in future trust the statements of the government rather than-I was going to say-the fabrications of our friends on the other side of the House. The immigration from the United States in 1908-9 was 59,832. In the first seven months of this year it was 65,755, or 6,000 more in seven months of this year than in the whole twelve months of last year. While this American immigration is a matter on congratulation for us, it is a matter over which the American people are very much alarmed. I was reading a few days ago an article in the Breeders ' Gazette ' of November 24, 1909, a leading agricultural paper published in Chicago, in which it is said:
An extraordinary gathering was the Land Congress in Chicago last week. The farm was the keynote, the farmer the man of the hour. Governors, senators, congressmen, land commissioners, scientific agriculturists, dry farmers, railroad immigration agents and others responded to the call in surprising numbers.
Again further on:
It was a notable _ gathering and not the least valuable of its influences is that directed against the loss of our farming population to Canada.
The ' Country Gentleman,' a leading agricultural paper published in Albany, New York, in its issue of November 25, last, says:
60,000	Americans went to Canada last year and took with them $60,000,000 to buy wheat lands in Canada.

In its issue of December 2, 1909, the same paper says:
The American emigration to the Canadian Northwest, after having some time ago aroused attention, has begun to excite alarm; and an association has been formed in Chicago to check it, with the motto, ' Why go to Canada ' The immediate occasion for concern is the announcement that the northward current has continued to flow this year all through the fall, instead of letting up as usual. In August, September and October 13,781 American settlers arrived in Winnipeg, 48 per cent more than were received in those three months of 1908. It is said that 500,000 Americans have crossed the border in the last ten years.
Referring to the motto of that Chicago congress, ' Why go to Canada?' I ask myself the question: Why do these American citizens, the very cream of the American farming population, and why do men in such large numbers from Britain and from the best parts of Europe, come to Canada? They come to Canada, in the first place, because of the natural advantages, the cheap lands we have to offer. They come, in the second place, because of the confidence they have in Canadian laws and the way in which we enforce our laws. They come in the third place, because this government, the Minister of the Interior, his deputy, the superintendent of immigration, and the Interior Department generally, have advertised in the most businesslike way the advantages which our country has to offer. So I say again that this government is entitled to the credit of bringing into the country the farmers who, the hon. member for North Toronto says, have saved the government and the country. Again I congratulate the Finance Minister upon the splendid budget which he has been able to present to-day and the splendid conditions which have enabled him so to do.
Mr. SPROULE moved the adjournment of the debate.
